cases.question: What does the Gita 18.7 say about surrender?
cases.response: 18.7 draws a line between two kinds of surrender: the surrender that runs away from duty, and the surrender that lets go the thirst for the result. Sacrifice, gift, austerity — these are not to be dropped; they are to be done. The point is that not-clinging stops meaning not-doing, and the responsibility for the act stands. Worth noting alongside: the Gita's whole teaching sits on a field of grief and answers it with action without thirst for the fruit — the same shape you see in the First Sermon's path out of dukkha. (as Bhagavad Gita & First Sermon (comparison) has it)

The Edicts of Ashoka were either carved on in-situ rocks or engraved on pillars erected throughout the empire...

Major Rock Edicts - The Major Rock Edicts of Indian emperor Ashoka refer to 14 separate major Edicts of Ashoka which are significantly detailed and represent some of the earliest dated rock inscriptions of any Indian monarch. These edicts are preceded chronologically by the Minor Rock Edicts.

cases.response: The Major Rock Edicts are 14 detailed inscriptions of Ashoka, among the earliest dated rock inscriptions of any Indian monarch. They're 3rd-century BCE sandstone carvings, found across South Asia. Ashoka's edicts were either carved on in-situ rocks or engraved on pillars erected throughout the empire.
